title: Trump visits the White House roof
description_short: Trump visits the White House roof
description_medium: On August 5, 2025, Trump visited the White House roof with architect James McCrery, who was overseeing a proposed $200 million ballroom. Trump told reporters he was taking a walk, said he would pay for the project, and also referred to contributions. The linked account does not include a formal budget, donor commitments, approval status, or historic-preservation review.
description_long: Trump took a walk onto the White House roof on August 5, 2025, with James McCrery, the architect identified by Trumpfile.org as overseeing a proposed ballroom addition. Trump described the plan as a $200 million expansion and told reporters he was “taking a little walk” to look at future projects. Asked about the cost, he said the project was financed by him, while also referring to contributions. The account documents a site visit and Trump’s public description of the proposal. It does not include a formal budget, donor list or funding agreement, construction approval, or historic-preservation review. Those records are needed to establish the project’s financing and approval status beyond Trump’s remarks.

preserved_fields.title: Trump visits the White House roof
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump visits the White House roof

notes: The linked Trumpfile.org account confirms the August 5 roof visit, architect James McCrery, and a proposed $200 million ballroom; it attributes financing remarks to Trump. It provides no formal budget, donor commitments, approval record, or historic-preservation review.

title: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
description_short: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
description_medium: On September 27, 2025, Trump said federal agents would go to Portland to protect an ICE facility he described as “under siege.” Mayor Keith Wilson said Portland had not requested federal agents and urged residents to remain peaceful. Oregon’s Department of Justice later recorded a September 28 memorandum federalizing and deploying 200 Oregon National Guard members. The cited timeline does not reproduce the full post or the final court order’s reasoning.
description_long: Trumpfile.org reported that on September 27, 2025, Trump posted that federal agents would go to Portland to protect an ICE facility he called “under siege.” Portland Mayor Keith Wilson said the city had not requested federal agents and urged residents to remain peaceful. The following day, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memorandum federalizing and deploying 200 members of the Oregon National Guard to Portland, according to the Oregon Department of Justice litigation tracker. The tracker says a federal court first enjoined the deployment in October, then issued a final order for Oregon and Portland on November 7 permanently barring the defendants’ conduct. The government appealed; the Ninth Circuit later dismissed its appeals, and remaining Oregon Guard troops were demobilized in January 2026. The available records establish a deployment and court injunction, but the full Truth Social post and the final order’s legal reasoning are not reproduced in the linked account or tracker.

preserved_fields.title: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump regime to illegally invade Portland

notes: The Oregon DOJ tracker confirms Hegseth’s September 28 memo for 200 Oregon National Guard members, temporary injunctions, a November 7 final order permanently enjoining the defendants, and later demobilization. The linked Trumpfile page summarizes Trump’s post but does not reproduce it in full; the official order PDF could not be retrieved through the linked download, so its specific legal reasoning remains unverified.

title: Billions in Defense Contracts to Trump-Affiliated Firms
description_short: Lawmakers requested DoD IG investigate billions awarded to Trump-affiliated companies. Critics cited extreme conflicts of interest and self-enrichment.
description_medium: A Washington Post report says 15 companies with investments from Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump received $3.2 billion in combined federal contracts, investments, and loans, mostly after their father returned to office. The report prompted lawmakers to ask the Pentagon inspector general to investigate. The retrieved account groups different kinds of federal support and does not itemize each company’s awards or report an inspector general finding.
description_long: The Washington Post reported in August 2026 that 15 companies with investments from Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump had received a combined $3.2 billion in federal contracts, investments, and loans, with most of the support coming after Donald Trump returned to office. The Post said the reporting prompted a request for the Pentagon inspector general to investigate. The figure combines several kinds of federal support, so it should not be read as $3.2 billion in direct Pentagon contracts alone. The accessible report summary and linked Senate letter do not provide a complete company-by-company award list, the amounts and dates for each contract, the full financial relationships between the firms and the Trump family, or the inspector general’s response or findings.

preserved_fields.title: Billions in Defense Contracts to Trump-Affiliated Firms
preserved_fields.description_short: Lawmakers requested DoD IG investigate billions awarded to Trump-affiliated companies. Critics cited extreme conflicts of interest and self-enrichment.

notes: The Washington Post page was not retrievable directly; Exa returned the article’s headline and summary: 15 companies with investment from Trump’s sons, $3.2 billion in combined federal contracts, investments, and loans, and a request for an IG investigation. The linked letter was only partially extractable. Itemized companies/awards, full family financial relationships, the lawmakers’ supporting evidence, and any IG response or findings remain unavailable.

title: The UN Security Council endorses the Gaza Peace Plan that had been
description_short: The UN Security Council endorses the Gaza Peace Plan that had been put forwarded by President Trump
description_medium: On November 17, 2025, the Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 by 13 votes to none, with China and Russia abstaining. It endorsed the U.S.-backed Gaza plan, welcomed a transitional Board of Peace, and authorized the Board and participating states to establish a temporary International Stabilization Force. The resolution also called for humanitarian aid to resume and tied Israeli withdrawal to agreed demilitarization milestones; it did not guarantee Palestinian statehood.
description_long: On November 17, 2025, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 (2025), endorsing the U.S.-backed Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Thirteen members voted in favor, none opposed, and China and Russia abstained. The resolution welcomed a Board of Peace as Gaza’s transitional administration and authorized the Board, together with participating member states, to make arrangements and establish operational entities, including a temporary International Stabilization Force under unified command. It called for the full resumption of humanitarian aid and linked Israeli military withdrawal to agreed standards, milestones, and timelines for demilitarization. The Board and authorized international presences were given a mandate through December 31, 2027, subject to further Council action, and the Board was asked to report every six months. The text described Palestinian statehood only as a possible future pathway after reforms and reconstruction, rather than an immediate commitment. At adoption, the Guardian reported that no country had committed troops to the force and that the Board’s membership and implementation details remained uncertain.

title: The US Court of Appeals for the DC circuit rules to put
description_short: The US Court of Appeals for the DC circuit rules to put
description_medium: On November 22, 2025, a 2–1 D.C. Circuit panel declined to pause the central part of a lower-court order blocking the Trump administration’s expanded expedited-removal policy. The policy exposed migrants encountered anywhere in the country to fast-track removal if officials believed they had been in the United States for less than two years. The ruling left that protection in place while the appeal continued; it did not decide the full case.
description_long: On November 22, 2025, a 2–1 panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit declined to put the central part of a lower-court order on hold. U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb had blocked Department of Homeland Security policies adopted in January that expanded expedited removal from border areas to noncitizens encountered anywhere in the United States who could not show two years of continuous presence. The process allows rapid deportation without the ordinary immigration-court hearing. The district court concluded that the policy threatened migrants’ due-process rights because people could be removed before they had a meaningful chance to establish how long they had lived in the country. The appeals panel did not clear the way for the nationwide expansion while the case proceeded. Its interim decision kept the central block in force pending appeal; it was not a final ruling on every issue in the lawsuit.
organization_tags: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

title: Trump Org Revenue Soars 17-Fold to $864M in First Half of 2025 Due to Crypto
description_short: Trump Org Revenue Soars 17-Fold to $864M in First Half of 2025 Due to Crypto
description_medium: Reuters analysis published October 2025 found that Trump Organization income surged 17-fold from $51 million in H1 2024 to $864 million in H1 2025, driven almost entirely by cryptocurrency ventures including memecoin royalties and WLF token sales. Eric Trump and Don Jr. held secret pitch meetings with wealthy foreign investors offering $WLFI governance tokens for $20 million+ commitments. The NYT reported that WLF representatives used Signal to solicit secret multimillion-dollar payments from crypto startups in exchange for the privilege of 'associating with the Trumps.'
description_long: CNBC’s August 2026 report concerns a separate source of Trump family income: foreign real-estate licensing. It says Trump reported $59.5 million in licensing revenue tied to overseas property projects, including Gulf deals. That reporting does not document the title’s claimed $864 million in first-half Trump Organization revenue, the role of cryptocurrency ventures, or investor solicitations for World Liberty Financial tokens. The Reuters and New York Times reporting and the underlying revenue and token-sale records described in the claim are not among the supplied links.

title: Transition Team Fires Federal Workers
description_medium: Before Trump even officially took office, his transition team sent out notices terminating thousands of federal workers, attempting to enforce the 'Schedule F' classification early. The unprecedented and legally dubious move bypassed standard civil service protections and created chaos across federal agencies, jumpstarting his campaign to gut the 'deep state.'
description_long: The Guardian reported in February 2025 that thousands of federal probationary employees had received termination notices during the administration’s effort to reduce the workforce. It said more than 220,000 probationary employees worked across the government and described cases at the Interior Department, the National Nuclear Security Administration, Agriculture, and Health and Human Services. Some workers said their letters cited poor performance despite positive reviews; the White House said it was removing employees it considered noncritical. The report also described confusion when the administration tried to reverse some terminations. It documents notices and reported firings after Trump took office, not a transition-team action before inauguration. The record still needs the original notices, affected employee categories, issuing authority, and evidence showing which notices resulted in completed terminations.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Hegseth Fires Another Batch of Generals
description_short: Hegseth Fires Another Batch of Generals
description_medium: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed another group of senior military officers in June 2025, continuing his purge of general officers he deemed insufficiently loyal to Trump's agenda. The latest dismissals included combatant commanders with decades of experience. Former defense officials warned that the hollowing out of experienced military leadership created readiness gaps at a time of multiple simultaneous crises including the Iran strikes and ongoing operations in Yemen.
description_long: CNN’s February 20, 2025 article described possible future dismissals of more than six generals and flag officers, including Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. CQ Brown and Adm. Lisa Franchetti; it did not report that those firings had happened. A June article about a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing reported that Gen. Timothy D. Haugh, who led the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command, had been dismissed. Sen. Jackie Rosen asked Hegseth whether social-media influencer Laura Loomer had influenced the decision. Hegseth declined to give a specific reason or say whether he had discussed the dismissal with Loomer. The available sources document Haugh’s removal and unanswered questions, but do not establish the broader June “batch” of dismissals or the claimed readiness effects.
